common_name: UFGold Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Non-Melting-Flesh Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; UFGold needs only about 200 chill hours, released by the University of Florida IFAS breeding program in 1997 for growers south of the traditional peach belt.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first couple of years to keep light reaching the interior wood. UFGold is a low-chill University of Florida release with firm, non-melting yellow flesh, a texture that holds up well for canning and preserving in addition to fresh eating, unlike the soft melting flesh of most low-chill dessert peaches. Its roughly 200-hour chill requirement lets it set a reliable crop through the mild winters typical of the Gulf Coast, where bloom on high-chill peach varieties is often erratic. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size, and watch for a hard late freeze during an unusually warm bloom period, since low-chill peaches can flower earlier than the local last-frost date in some years.

common_name: Sunraycer Nectarine (Low-Chill Nectarine for Warm Winters)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunraycer needs only about 250-300 chill hours, letting it set fruit reliably through mild Gulf Coast winters. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with deep, well-drained soil; nectarines share peach culture but their smooth skin makes them more prone to fruit-scarring insects and bacterial spot, so a warm-humid Gulf Coast planting benefits from an open, breezy site. Sunraycer sets a heavy early crop of medium-to-large fruit with bright red skin and sweet-tart yellow flesh, typically ripening ahead of most peaches in the same yard. Thin fruit clusters to one nectarine every 4-6 inches once they reach marble size to prevent limb breakage and improve final fruit size, and prune annually to an open, low vase shape after harvest to renew the one-year wood nectarines fruit on.

common_name: Suncoast Nectarine (University of Florida Low-Chill Nectarine for the Gulf Coast)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; Suncoast was released by the University of Florida in 1995 with a chill requirement of roughly 250-300 hours, suiting it to north Florida, south Alabama, and nearby Gulf Coast gardens. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, siting them where good air movement helps foliage dry quickly after Gulf Coast humidity and rain. Suncoast is a University of Florida low-chill release with yellow, semi-clingstone flesh, a red blush covering most of the fruit, and notably better resistance to bacterial spot on leaves and fruit than many older nectarine varieties, an important trait in humid growing conditions where bacterial spot is a persistent problem. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set, and expect harvest in late April to early May, among the earliest tree fruit of the season in a Gulf Coast garden.

common_name: Scarlet Beauty Plum (Ultra-Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Deep Gulf South)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Scarlet Beauty needs only about 150 chill hours, among the lowest of any named plum, making it reliable even in the warmest Gulf Coast winters. Self-fertile, but fruit set and size improve with a nearby low-chill Japanese plum pollinator such as Gulf Beauty or Gulf Blaze.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, since plum roots decline quickly in standing water. Developed by a Florida plant breeder for the state's mildest winters, Scarlet Beauty carries one of the lowest chill requirements of any Japanese-type plum, letting it flower and set fruit dependably where higher-chill plums bloom sparsely or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized with red-streaked amber flesh and ripens in May, ahead of most other plums in the same garden. Thin fruit clusters when marble-sized to reduce limb breakage and improve fruit size, and plant a second low-chill Japanese plum nearby to boost yields even though the tree is partly self-fruitful.

common_name: Gulfbeauty Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Gulfbeauty needs roughly 225 chill hours, one of the University of Florida's 'Gulf' series bred for warm-winter fruit reliability. Plant with another low-chill Japanese plum, such as Gulfblaze or Gulfrose, for the best fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil. Gulfbeauty is one of the University of Florida's 'Gulf' series of Japanese-type plums bred with resistance to bacterial spot and plum leaf scald, two disease pressures that are common in the humid Gulf South and that can devastate plums selected for drier western growing regions. The 1.5-2 inch fruit has red skin and good eating quality, and the tree typically ripens its crop in May, roughly two weeks ahead of plums grown farther north. Thin developing fruit to a few inches apart once set to improve final size, and plant a second Gulf-series plum nearby to raise yields, since cross-pollination improves fruit set even on trees described as self-fruitful.

common_name: Gulfblaze Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Gulfblaze needs roughly 250 chill hours, part of the University of Florida's low-chill 'Gulf' series bred for warm-winter reliability. Plant with another low-chill Japanese plum, such as Gulfbeauty or Gulfrose, for the best fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, away from low spots where cold air and moisture pool. Gulfblaze is part of the University of Florida's 'Gulf' series of low-chill Japanese plums, bred alongside Gulfbeauty and Gulfrose with resistance to bacterial spot and plum leaf scald, both significant problems for plum growers in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Fruit has bright red skin and ripens in the same early-to-late May window as its Gulf-series siblings, giving Gulf Coast gardeners fresh plums well ahead of the general plum season. Thin fruit to a few inches apart once set, and interplant with a second Gulf-series plum to improve pollination and overall yield.

common_name: Au Producer Plum (Auburn University High-Yielding Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Upper Gulf South)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Au Producer requires a cross-pollinator, such as another Auburn 'Au' series plum or Methley, within about 50 feet. Its chill requirement of roughly 650-700 hours is higher than most Gulf series plums, making it best suited to zone 8 and the cooler parts of zone 9 rather than the warmest coastal microclimates.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, since Prunus species decline quickly with wet feet. Au Producer was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station in 1977 as a high-yielding early-season plum, part of the Auburn 'Au' series of Japanese-American hybrids bred to combine the disease tolerance of native American plum with the fruit quality of Japanese plum for the humid Southeast. The clingstone fruit has purple skin and sweet, juicy red flesh good for fresh eating and canning, and the tree carries strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial leaf spot, and bacterial canker, diseases that trouble many plum varieties in Gulf South humidity. Because its moderate chill requirement is higher than the ultra-low-chill 'Gulf' series plums, Au Producer performs most reliably in zone 8 gardens and should be evaluated cautiously in the warmest parts of zone 9.

scientific_name: Citrus paradisi x Poncirus trifoliata x Citrus sinensis 'US-119'

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; US-119 is a USDA hybrid combining citrumelo (grapefruit x trifoliate orange) and sweet orange parentage, and mature wood has reportedly tolerated brief dips to around 15°F with limited damage, considerably colder than a standard sweet orange survives.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a protected spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter buffering in zone 8-9 gardens. US-119 was developed by USDA breeders from a cross of citrumelo and sweet orange, giving it roughly one-quarter trifoliate orange parentage and correspondingly greater cold tolerance than a true sweet orange, while retaining a genuinely sweet, orange-like flavor rather than the sharp bitterness typical of many trifoliate hybrids. Fruit has a smooth, attractive orange peel, relatively few seeds, and juicy flesh with just a hint of the trifoliate parent's distinctive aftertaste. Because of its unusual hardiness for citrus with real dessert-orange flavor, it has become popular among cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing sweet citrus north of the traditional growing range; protect young trees through their first few winters, since mature specimens are considerably tougher.
